fusion_ranked_evidence.title: Supreme Court: Dismissal of S.482 CrPC Petition Does not Bar Next Petition Filed Due To Change In Law
fusion_ranked_evidence.snippet: The State of Punjab, Criminal Appeal No. 5491/2024** on December 19, 2024,  held that the dismissal of a petition filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (“**Cr.P.C.**”) does not prevent the accused from filing a subsequent petition filed due to a change in the law, even without seeking specific liberty in the earlier petition. The Appellants challenged the direction of the deposit of 20% (twenty percent) of the compensation amount, which was a condition for suspension of the sentence following their conviction under Section 138 of the N.I. Act, by way of a Petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. 6. In this exclusive conversation, Legal Reporter Editor Viplava Awasthi speaks with Advocate Vikas Gupta on the crucial powers of the High Court under Section 482 of CrPC and Section 528 of the newly enacted BNSS.
The discussion revolves around the High Court’s inherent powers to quash false or malicious FIRs, and the recent Supreme Court judgment in the Pradeep Keserwani case, where a clear 4-point litmus test has been laid down.

This interview is highly informative for lawyers, law students, and the general public who want to understand when and how an FIR can be quashed by the High Court.

Power of High Court under Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS
